Voat has been through a lot of the course of these past years, but its mantra and motive have remained the same: Have your say. Speech shall not be suppressed so ideas will not be lost. Discussion will reign supreme. An inspiring backbone for a website in this modern world. Thanks to the hard work and morality from the admins and the support of the community we have been able to maintain this position.

There have been controversies and there have been concerns. Rogue mods, missing admins. The drama can seem almost cyclical, like history, at times.

I just wanted to make a post about where Voat stands now with regards to freedom. The concerns that I have heard raised are many, but primarily include the power of downvotes, the power of moderators, the power of admins, and the power of the mob.

To me the power of downvotes singly is a non-issue. If a single comment gets downvoted enough it will collapse, but this is not censorship. The comment can still be read by all, and oftentimes I find it will be read more than other average-score comments, because people are drawn to the controversial. Even if people use downvotes as disagree buttons to the point that unpopular individual comments are collapsed, this is not censorship. Usually only obnoxious comments will be collapsed in this way, but opinions can get hit by it too. Individually this is a non-issue.

The power of moderators is annoying, but justifiable. In order for a website such as Voat to have any organization or usability at all, content must be organized, which is why we have subverses. If subverses get flooded with content not meant for them, moderators can remove that content. Personally I believe no (legal) content should ever be deleted from Voat; if content does not belong in a subverse it should be removed from that subverse and re-posted in a subverse like /v/whatever or /v/removed. This way we can maintain an organized community and avoid all cries of censorship. Of course if a moderator stops serving the ends of the subverse and goes rogue, that is a mis-use of power and that moderator can simply be replaced. Still not censorship, still not an infringement of freedom. The moderator is free to start their own community and run it their way, but not free to betray an existing community and use it for their own ends.

The power of admins is supreme, of course, but the moral strength of @Atko and @PuttItOut have helped keep Voat on the right path. This is not to say they are without some flaws; we are all flawed. Actions can be taken imperfectly or inefficiently, but what is special about our admins is that they listen to the community, they care about the community, and they learn from actions that turn out to be unpopular. They are responsible, in other words, and as I said in my recent post about Putt's bannings so far, I think the trend of their responsibility will only continue.

The power of the mob. This is the only aspect of Voat where I feel we may actually be missing a mark or two. The recent update to stop vote manipulators has made good headway to prevent this kind of abuse, but we are still not totally free in this way. You see, in the hypothetical situation where a user posts nothing but unpopular opinions, not for the sake of stirring up trouble, but simply because that is where their interests lie and that is what they believe, and if that user does so in a non-inflammatory, non-disrespectful way, it is still possible for that user for accrue enough downvotes to be actually censored on Voat. If they never gained enough CCP to vote or contribute effectively to begin with this is even more possible. Such a situation is so improbable you may deem it not worth mentioning, but because actual censorship is possible on Voat I feel the need to mention it. We're talking about an innocent person censored because of their ideas alone.

My only question to you, and the primary point of this post, is to ask why?

Why are negative CCP restrictions necessary? What do they accomplish? The only people they truly hurt are established users. Spammers who would ordinarily be thwarted by -CCP restrictions could just create a new account and continue on, while a user who has established a place in a community or a style or whathaveyou might be censored and have to start over. With the recent changes I think there may even be limits to the number of accounts on a single IP in which case an unfortunate person could join Voat, make a few posts about their unpopular opinions without even necessarily realizing that their views are unpopular, they would reach substantial limits on their accounts, and then be unable to create a new account without the use of a VPN.

If we are going to limit accounts based on IP addresses, or some derivative of that method, why have negative CCP restrictions at all, the only true form of anti-freedom I can detect throughout all of Voat? Why not just ban accounts who are made and then begin to spam immediately (for breaking Voat rules and themselves being anti-freedom, just as we ban vote manipulators now) and make the imaginary internet points irrelevant in the negatives. A person with -1000 CCP could hold a civil discussion with someone with 1000 CCP without issue or any justification for claims of censorship.

Shit this was a long post. PuttItOut I didn't tag you meaninglessly; I was hoping you might weigh in. I was also hoping the community might do the same. If people think that the restrictions are totally justified, despite the potential for anti-freedom on Voat, I would love to hear the argument. I'm not set in stone on my beliefs here.

Thanks for reading. If you agree or disagree, please reply so we can have a discussion about this as a community.
The State of Voat and its Relation with Freedom

Well, it is a little more nuanced than that. The primary spillway (concrete riverbed) developed a hole which then allowed the released water to start eroding the earth around the spillway. The erosion had started working its way up the hill toward the primary spillway gates threatening the gates integrity. This forced them to cut back on the primary spillway flow which then allowed the lake to rise to the secondary spillway (essentially a concrete rim that allows the lake to overflow). Erosion at the base of the emergency spillway also proved significant and was working its way up toward the rim. If the erosion compromised the rim cap then the entire spillway area could fail causing an uncontrolled release of about 30 feet of the lakes water. So while not the full 770 feet of the primary dam it's still a huge volume of water. Enough to wash away anything immediately downstream.

Fortunately they managed to up the primary spillway flow without significant new erosion droping the lake level below the secondary spillway. The big problem now is they are forecasting another significant rainfall starting Wednesday.
